reasoning_traces.think:
The core tension in perfect competition lies in balancing voluntary agreement efficiency against external effects. When individuals act solely on self-interest without accounting for externalities, the system fails to maximize total social advantage. This creates two failure regimes: one where agreements fall short due to unaccounted benefits (e.g., land development), and another where they exceed optimal levels due to unmitigated costs (e.g., pollution). These dynamics suggest that the mechanical effectiveness of free contract depends critically on how well it accounts for indirect impacts. The ethical foundation of reward systems further complicates matters by requiring explicit alignment between compensation and performance. Thus, the derivation reveals that efficient markets require both bounded rationality and structured feedback mechanisms to correct for systemic biases.
